title: A-L-M
hookLine: olam, world, and ne'elam, hidden: Hasidic teachers say the world hides God

cards: A small boy runs into his grandfather's study, crying. He'd been playing hide-and-seek. He found a good spot, hid, and waited.
And waited. When he finally came out, he found that his friend had stopped looking long ago and wandered off.

In the version people tell, the grandfather is a Hasidic rabbi, Rabbi Baruch of Medzhybizh, and when he hears it, he begins to cry too. God says the same thing, he tells the boy. I hide, and no one comes looking.

teach.b: A-L-M. Ayin, lamed, mem. Olam: world.
And ne'elam: hidden. First, time. In the Bible olam can reach toward time more than space: le-olam, forever.
A psalm repeats it as a refrain, line after line: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Olam is a stretch so long you can't see its far end. Second, hidden.
In Leviticus, a person touches something unclean, "and if it be hidden from him." The Hebrew is ne'lam, from these letters: something real that the person can't see.

teach.h: THE WORLD SET IN THEIR HEART.
teach.b: Third, Kohelet sets the word inside us: God "hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end."
The word there is ha-olam, and readers have heard it as the world, or eternity, or something hidden: something vast placed in a person that they can't get to the end of. Fourth, the Hasidic teachers.

teach.h: THE WORLD AS A HIDING PLACE.
teach.b: They read the shared letters as a teaching: the world, olam, is the place where God is ne'elam, hidden. Creation is a kind of hiding place.
Notice the difference between hidden and gone. Hidden means someone is there to be found. That's why the grandfather cried.

how: Hasidic teachers read olam, world, together with he'elem, hiddenness, and teach that the world both conceals God and invites seeking; a Hasidic story tells of a child whose friend stopped looking for him in hide-and-seek.

o: the Hebrew root of a mountain or height
the Hebrew root of world, and of hidden
the Hebrew root of silence, being mute

p: God says the same: I hide

s: in the Bible, olam can mean forever
le-olam: "for his mercy endureth for ever."
the Hasidic teaching says God is absent from the world
hidden, not absent: hiding means someone is there to be found.
Kohelet says no one can find out God's work from beginning to end
God "hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work."

games.q: you're the boy. you've found a perfect hiding spot, and you've waited a long time. nobody comes. what do you do?
o: come out, and find your friend stopped looking.
games.why: he comes out to find nobody looking, and runs crying to his grandfather, who says God says the same: I hide, and no one comes looking.

practice: Close your eyes and listen for the sounds under the obvious ones, a fridge humming, a bird, a car far off, your own breath.
Then open them, choose one ordinary object near you, and ask what's hidden in it: the hands that made it, the ground it came from, the road it took to reach you.
If you pray, the looking itself can be a kind of seeking; if you don't, let it simply be seeing.

wordCard.voice: A-L-M. Ayin, lamed, mem: olam, the world and forever, and ne'elam, hidden. A hiding place with someone in it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: world, and in older texts forever, from ayin, lamed, mem; ne'elam, hidden, shares the letters.

carryVoice: Your line: the world hides. A game of hide-and-seek only works if somebody goes looking. Back tomorrow, same hill.
